Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 31, verses 6–7:

Al-Wahidi and others said: Most commentators hold that what is meant by *lahw al-hadith* (idle talk) is singing (*ghina'*). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, in the transmission of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Miqsam from him, and by 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, in the transmission of Abu al-Sahba' from him. It is also the view of Mujahid and 'Ikrimah.

Thawr ibn Abi Fakhtah narrated from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding the words of the Most High: ﴿And among people is one who purchases idle talk﴾. He said: "It is the man who buys a slave girl who sings to him by night and by day."

Ibn Abi Najih narrated from Mujahid: "It is buying a singer, male or female, for a large sum of money, and listening to them, and to the like of them of falsehood."

This is also the view of Makhul, and it is the choice of Abu Ishaq as well.

He said: The most that has come in the tafsir is that *lahw al-hadith* here is singing, because it diverts from the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted.

Al-Wahidi said: The people of meanings (*ahl al-ma'ani*) said: Included in this is everyone who chooses diversion, singing, musical instruments, and wind instruments over the Qur'an. Although the wording mentions purchase, the term "purchase" is used for exchange and choice, and this is common in the Qur'an.

He said: What supports this is what Qatadah said regarding this verse: "Perhaps he has not spent any wealth," and he said: "It is enough of misguidance for a person that he prefers the talk of falsehood over the talk of truth."

Al-Wahidi said: This verse, on this interpretation, indicates the prohibition of singing. Then he mentioned al-Shafi'i's statement on rejecting the testimony of one who publicly engages in singing.

He said: As for the singing of *qaynat* (singing slave girls), that is the gravest matter in this category, because of the many severe warnings concerning it. It was narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever listens to a *qaynah* (singing girl), molten lead will be poured into his ears on the Day of Resurrection."

*Al-Anuk*: molten lead.

The interpretation of *lahw al-hadith* as singing has also come traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ).

In the *Musnad* of Imam Ahmad, the *Musnad* of 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr al-Humaydi, and the *Jami' al-Tirmidhi*, from the hadith of Abu Umamah, and the wording is that of al-Tirmidhi: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do not sell *qaynat* (singing girls), do not buy them, and do not teach them. There is no good in trade involving them, and their price is unlawful."

It is concerning the like of this that this verse was revealed: ﴿And among people is one who purchases idle talk, to mislead from the way of Allah﴾ [Luqman: 6].

Although the transmission of this hadith revolves around 'Ubaydullah ibn Zahr, from 'Ali ibn Yazid al-Ilhani, from al-Qasim, and 'Ubaydullah ibn Zahr is trustworthy, al-Qasim is trustworthy, and 'Ali is weak, the hadith has corroborating evidences and supporting chains, which we will mention if Allah wills. It is sufficient that the Companions and the Successors interpreted *lahw al-hadith* as singing, for this is authentically reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud.

Abu al-Sahba' said: "I asked Ibn Mas'ud about the words of the Most High: ﴿And among people is one who purchases idle talk﴾ [Luqman: 6], and he said: 'By Allah, besides whom there is no god, it is singing,' repeating it three times."

It is also authentically reported from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it is singing.

Al-Hakim Abu 'Abdullah said in the tafsir section of his *al-Mustadrak*: "Let the seeker of this knowledge know that the tafsir of a Companion who witnessed the revelation and the descent is, according to the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), a hadith with a continuous chain (*musnad*)."

He said in another place in his book: "It is, in our view, in the category of the raised (*marfu'*) hadith."

Although there is room for scrutiny in this, there is no doubt that it is more deserving of acceptance than the tafsir of those after them, for they are the most knowledgeable of the Ummah about what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, intends by His Book. It was revealed to them, and they were the first of the Ummah to be addressed by it.

They witnessed its interpretation from the Messenger (ﷺ), in knowledge and in practice, and they were truly eloquent Arabs. Therefore, one should not depart from their tafsir where a way to it is found.

There is no contradiction between interpreting *lahw al-hadith* as singing and interpreting it as the reports of non-Arabs and their kings, the kings of Rome, and the like, which al-Nadr ibn al-Harith used to narrate to the people of Makkah, occupying them with it away from the Qur'an. Both are *lahw al-hadith*. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas said: "*Lahw al-hadith*: falsehood and singing."

So among the Companions some mentioned this, some mentioned the other, and some combined both.

Singing is more diverting and greater in harm than the stories and reports of kings, for it is the incantation of fornication, the breeding ground of hypocrisy, the snare of Satan, the intoxicant of the intellect, and its diversion from the Qur'an is greater than the diversion caused by other false speech, because of the strong inclination of souls toward it and their desire for it.

Having established this, those who engage in singing and those who listen to it have a share of this censure in proportion to their preoccupation with singing away from the Qur'an, even if they do not receive all of it. The verses include the censure of one who substitutes idle talk for the Qur'an, to mislead from the way of Allah without knowledge, and takes it as a mockery. When the Qur'an is recited to him, he turns away arrogantly as if he had not heard it, as if there were deafness in his ears, meaning heaviness and deafness. When he learns something of it, he mocks it. The combination of this only occurs in the greatest of people in disbelief. Even if some of it occurs in singers and their listeners, they have a share and portion of this censure.

This is clarified by the fact that you will not find anyone who is preoccupied with singing and the listening to its instruments except that there is in him straying from the path of guidance, in knowledge and in practice, and a turning away from listening to the Qur'an toward listening to singing. So much so that when the opportunity for listening to singing and listening to the Qur'an presents itself, he turns from the latter to the former, the Qur'an becomes burdensome to him, and circumstances may lead him to make the reciter fall silent and to lengthen his own listening, and to seek more of the singer and to consider his own turn too short. At the very least, he will receive a considerable share of this censure, even if he does not receive all of it.

The discussion on this is addressed to the one who has within his heart some life that he feels.

As for the one whose heart has died and whose trial has grown great, he has closed for himself the path of advice:

﴿And whoever Allah wants to test, you cannot avail him against Allah at all. Those are the ones for whom Allah does not desire to purify their hearts. For them in this world is disgrace, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41].

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 31, verse 11:

The words of the Most High: ﴿This is the creation of Allah; so show me what those other than Him have created﴾

How sweet and concise this expression is, and how clearly it proves the falsehood of association (shirk)! For if they claim that their deities created anything alongside Allah, they are challenged to show it to them.

And if they acknowledge that these deities are weaker, more powerless, and less than that, then their divinity is false and impossible.

(Benefit)

When the verse was revealed, "Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing (ẓulm), those are the ones who will have security, and they are the guided" (Al-An'am: 82),

the Companions said: "O Messenger of Allah, which of us has not mixed his belief with wrongdoing?" He said: "That is shirk (polytheism). Have you not heard the words of the righteous servant: 'Indeed, shirk is a great wrongdoing (ẓulm)' (Luqman: 13)?"

When the meaning of "wrongdoing" became unclear to them, and they thought that wronging oneself was included in it, and that whoever wrongs himself, in any way, would not be secure, he answered them that the wrongdoing which absolutely removes security and guidance is shirk.

By Allah, this is the answer that heals the sick and quenches the thirst.

For absolute and complete wrongdoing is shirk, which is placing worship in other than its proper place. Absolute security and guidance is security in this world and the Hereafter, and guidance to the straight path. So absolute and complete wrongdoing prevents absolute security and guidance. That does not prevent that general wrongdoing may prevent general security and general guidance, so reflect on this.

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on surah 31, verse 17:

His command to what is right (al-ma'ruf) encompasses his own doing of it and his commanding others to do it; likewise his forbidding of what is wrong (al-munkar).

As far as the literal wording goes, he himself is included in it, along with others.

As for the necessity established by the Sharia, the one who commands and forbids cannot have his commanding and forbidding stand sound unless he is himself the first one commanded and the first one forbidden.

And Allah, glorified is He, mentioned these three principles in His saying: ﴿Only those of understanding remember (19) Those who fulfil the covenant of Allah and do not break the binding agreement (20) And those who join what Allah has ordered to be joined, and fear their Lord and dread a terrible account (21) And those who patiently seek the countenance of their Lord, establish prayer, spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly, and repel evil with good; those – for them is the good outcome of the Home (22)﴾.

(Section)

Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: Abd al-Warith ibn Sufyan informed us, Qasim ibn Asbagh narrated to us, Abu al-Zanba' Rawh ibn al-Faraj narrated to us:

Sa'id ibn 'Ufayr and Abd al-Aziz ibn Yahya al-Madani narrated to us, Malik ibn Anas narrated to us from Ibn Shihab from Isma'il ibn Muhammad ibn Thabit al-Ansari from Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him:

"O Thabit, are you not pleased to live praiseworthy, to be killed a martyr, and to enter Paradise?"

Malik said: Thabit ibn Qays was then killed as a martyr on the day of Yamama.

Abu 'Umar said: Hisham ibn 'Ammar narrated from Sadaqa ibn Khalid, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid ibn Jabir narrated to us, saying: 'Ata' al-Khurasani told me, saying: Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas's daughter told me, she said: When there was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾

Her father entered his house and closed its door upon himself, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) missed him and sent for him, asking him about his condition.

He said: "I am a man with a loud voice; I fear that my deeds have been nullified."

He said: "No, you are not one of them; rather you will live well and die well."

She said: Then Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love everyone self-deluded and boastful﴾, so he closed his door upon himself and began to weep. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) missed him, so he sent for him and he informed him. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I love beauty, and I love that my people should be chiefs."

He said: "You are not one of them; rather you will live praiseworthy, be killed a martyr, and enter Paradise."

She said: When the day of Yamama came, he went out with Khalid ibn al-Walid against Musaylima. When they met and [the Muslims] were routed, Thabit and Salim, the freedman of Abu Hudhayfa, said: "This is not how we used to fight alongside the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Then each of them dug a pit for himself, and the people charged at them, but they stood firm and fought until they were killed. On Thabit that day was a precious coat of mail; a man from the Muslims passed by him and took it.

While a man among the Muslims was sleeping, [Thabit] came to him in his dream and said to him:

"I charge you with a bequest. Beware of saying, 'This is merely a dream,' and neglecting it. When I was killed, a man from the Muslims passed by me and took my coat of mail. His dwelling is at the farthest end of the people, and by his tent there is a horse pulling at its tether in its long rope. He has overturned a cooking pot over my coat of mail and placed a saddle atop the pot. Go to Khalid ibn al-Walid and tell him to send for my coat of mail and take it. And when you come to the Caliph of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) (meaning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq), say to him: 'Upon me is such-and-such debt, and I am owed such-and-such debt, and such-and-such of my slaves is freed, and such-and-such.'"

The man went to Khalid and informed him, and he sent for the coat of mail and it was brought. He also told Abu Bakr of his vision, and [Abu Bakr] executed his bequest.

[Abu 'Umar] said: We know of no one whose bequest was executed after his death other than Thabit ibn Qays, may Allah have mercy on him. End of what Abu 'Umar mentioned.

Khalid, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, and the Companions with him thus agreed to act upon this dream, to execute the bequest in accordance with it, and to take the coat of mail from the one who held it on that basis. This is pure jurisprudence (al-fiqh al-mahd).

And if Abu Hanifa, Ahmad and Malik accept the claim of one of the spouses regarding what is suitable to them and not the other, on the basis of evidence of its truthfulness, then this is more deserving [of acceptance].

Likewise, Abu Hanifa accepts the claim of one who claims a wall by the presence of bricks alongside it and by the knots of its binding ("«1»").

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on surah 31, verse 27:

He informs that His words do not run out, because of His might (*'izza*) and His wisdom (*hikma*). These are two essential attributes of Him, glorified and exalted, and He cannot be other than that.

Ibn Abi Hatim (d. 327 AH), in his *Tafsir*, reported on the authority of Sulayman ibn Amir, who said: I heard al-Rabi' ibn Anas say:

"The knowledge of all the servants, in comparison with the knowledge of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is like a single drop from all these seas. Allah, glorified and exalted, has revealed concerning this: ﴿And if whatever trees on earth were pens and the sea [were ink], replenished thereafter by seven seas...﴾ (31:27), and His saying: ﴿Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted...﴾ (18:109)."

He, glorified and exalted, says: "Say: If the sea were ink for the words of Allah, and all the trees were pens, the pens would break and the water of the sea would run out, while the words of Allah, exalted is He, remain. Nothing can exhaust them, because no one can measure His measure or praise Him as He deserves; rather, He is as He praised Himself."

"Our Lord is as He says, and beyond what He says."

In *al-Sawa'iq al-Mursalah* he said:

"So the ocean that encircles the world is measured as ink, and beyond it are seven other seas encircling it all, as ink with which the words of Allah are written. The seas would run dry and the pens would perish, even if all the trees of the earth from the time of their creation until the end of the world were measured, and the words of Allah would not be exhausted."

(Chapter)

*Lau* (لو, a conditional particle) is used to link one past event to another past event, as when you say: "If you had visited me, I would have honored you" (*lau zurtani la-akramtuka*). For this reason it does not put a following present-tense verb in the jussive mood, because it is origin-

ally for the past, both in form and in meaning. As in "If Zayd had visited me, I would have honored him" (*lau yazurani Zayd la-akramtuhu*). In its conditional function it is like *in* (إن, "if") in linking two clauses, but not in governing (*'amal*) or in referring to the future.

Some of the later scholars, namely Taj al-Din al-Kindi, denied that *lau* is a conditional particle, and he considered al-Zamakhshari mistaken in counting it among the conditional particles. Al-Andalusi said in his commentary on *al-Mufassal*: "I related this to our shaykh Abu al-Baqa', and he said: Taj al-Din erred in this criticism, for *lau* links one thing to another just as *in* does. The dispute may be verbal. If by the conditional one means the non-material, judgmental link, then the correct view is what Abu al-Baqa' and al-Zamakhshari said. If by the conditional one means what governs both clauses, then it is not one of the conditional particles."

Eighth issue: It is well known that when *lau* enters upon two affirmative clauses, it negates them both; when it enters upon two negative clauses, it affirms them both; and when it enters upon a negative and an affirmative, it affirms the negated and negates the affirmed. This is because it indicates the impossibility of one thing due to the impossibility of another. When the negation is impossible, it becomes an affirmation, so the four cases arise. Several objections have been raised to this.

The first is the verse: ﴿And if whatever trees on earth were pens and the sea [were ink], replenished thereafter by seven seas, the words of Allah would not be exhausted.﴾ (31:27)

According to what you have stated, the words of Allah would have been exhausted, and that is impossible. For the first clause is an affirmation, namely that the trees of the earth are pens and the seas are ink for His words, and this is negated. And the second clause, "the words of Allah would not be exhausted," would then have to be an affirmation.

The second is the saying of Umar: "What an excellent servant Suhayb is; if he did not fear Allah, he would not disobey Him." This has no basis. According to your rule, fear would be affirmed, since it is negated, and disobedience would be likewise affirmed, since it is also negated. People have given varied answers to this.

Abu al-Hasan ibn Asfur said: *lau* in the hadith means *in* (إن, "if"), for mere linking, so its negation is not an affirmation nor its affirmation a negation, and the objection is resolved. But there is considerable weakness in this answer, for the hadith does not intend mere linking, as he said. It intends a linking that includes the negation of the consequence, and the speech was not brought for anything else. So the answer nullifies the special property of *lau* by which it differs from the other conditional particles.

Another said: *lau* in the language is for mere linking, and it became well known in common usage for turning an affirmation into a negation and vice versa. The hadith came in the sense of the language. This answer was related by Muhammad al-Qarafi from al-Khasr Shahi, and it is far more corrupt than the previous one. For *lau*'s implication of negating what follows it and affirming what is negated is derived from its original positing, not from newly established usage. Just as the meanings of all other particles, whether negation, emphasis, restriction, explanation, beginning, or ending, are derived from their positing and not from usage. So what he said is manifestly false.

The third is the answer of Shaykh Abu Muhammad ibn Abd al-Salam and others: a single thing may have one cause, so it is negated when that cause is negated; or it may have two causes, so the absence of one does not entail the absence of the thing, because the second cause takes the place of the first. As in our saying about a husband who is also a paternal cousin: "If he were not a husband, he would inherit," namely by agnatic succession (*ta'sib*). For these are two causes, and the absence of one does not entail the absence of the other. Likewise, people here, for the most part, refrained from disobedience only out of fear; when fear leaves them, they disobey, because the cause is singular in their case. So Umar informed that Suhayb had two causes restraining him from disobedience: fear and reverence. If fear were absent in his case, disobedience would still be absent because of the other cause, namely reverence. This is a great praise for him.

I say: this same answer applies to the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying about the daughter of Hamzah: "Indeed, if she were not my stepdaughter in my guardianship, she would still be unlawful to me, for she is the daughter of my brother through fosterage." Related by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

That is, there are two causes requiring the prohibition. If one of them were supposed absent, the prohibition would not be absent, because of the second cause. This is a very good answer.

The fourth answer was mentioned by some scholars, who said: the apodosis of *lau* is omitted, and its estimated form is: "If he did not fear Allah, He would protect him," so he did not disobey Him, through His affection for him. For Allah protects His servant sometimes through fear and sometimes through love and reverence. But the protection through love and reverence is greater than the protection through fear, because fear is connected to His punishment, while love and reverence are connected to His essence and to what He, blessed and exalted, deserves. How can one of them be compared with the other? For this reason, the religion of love is more firm and enduring than the religion of fear, more effective and more powerful in influence. The evidence is what we see of the obedience of the lover to the beloved and the obedience of the fearful to the one he fears. As one of the Companions said: "Indeed, [his] love draws from me obedience that fear does not draw." This is not the place to expand on this matter, which is of great significance, and I have expanded on it in my book *al-Futuhat al-Qudsiyya*.

The fifth: the original use of *lau* is to link two things, as mentioned before. Then it may also be used to break a link. It then becomes an answer to a real or imagined question in which a link has been made, and you break it because you believe that link to be false. As when someone says: "If Zayd is not a husband, he does not inherit," and you reply: "If he were not a husband, Zayd would still inherit," meaning that the link he made between non-marriage and non-inheritance is not true. Your intention is to cut the link of his speech, not to link it. Similarly, you may say: "If Zayd were not learned, he would still be honored," meaning for his bravery, as an answer to a questioner who imagines that if he were not learned he would not be honored. You link the absence of learning with honor, and you cut that link. It is not your intention to link the absence of learning with honor, because that is not appropriate, nor is it among the aims of rational people, and your speech only makes sense as a denial of the link. Likewise, in the hadith: since the usual tendency of people is to link their disobedience with their lack of fear, and this link is in their imaginations, Umar cut this link and said, "If he did not fear Allah, he would not disobey Him." Similarly, since the usual imagination is that if all the trees became pens and all the seas were ink for writing the divine words, then perhaps the imagination would say: nothing is written with this except that it is exhausted, whatever it may be. So Allah, exalted is He, cut this link and negated this imagination, saying: "...would not be exhausted."

I say: a parallel to this in the hadith is that his wife imagined that the daughter of his paternal uncle Hamzah was lawful to him because she was his uncle's daughter. So he cut this link by saying that she was not lawful, and he mentioned two causes for the prohibition: fosterage and her being his stepdaughter. This is al-Qarafi's answer. He said: "It is better than the previous answers in two respects. First, it covers both the hadith and the verse, whereas some of the previous answers do not apply to the verse. Second, that *lau* means *in* is contrary to the apparent meaning, whereas what he mentioned does not involve departing from the apparent meaning."

I say: there is much to be said against this answer. If he claims that *lau* was posited, or brought, to cut a link, then he is mistaken, for it is one of the conditional particles, whose content is to link a cause with its effect and a necessitating thing with its necessary consequence. It was not brought to cut this connection, nor was it posited for that at all. So a particle should not be explained by the opposite of its positing. A parallel to this is the saying of someone who claims that *illa* (إلا, "except") can mean *wa* (الواو, "and"). This is false, for *wa* is for association and conjunction, while *illa* is for exclusion, and it cuts association and similar things. If he means that the cutting of a supposed link is an intention of the speaker drawn from evidence, then this is true. But it does not arise from the particle *lau*. It comes from the specific context accompanying it, which includes the negation of what the speaker imagined or claimed, and not from *lau* itself.

This is what these excellent scholars said on this question.

The difficulty arose, both as question and answer, from a lack of comprehensive understanding of the meaning of this particle, its implication, and its reality. I will now mention the reality of this particle so that the secret of the matter becomes clear, by the help of Allah.

(*Lau* is for necessary connection between two things.)

Know that *lau* is a particle posited for the necessary connection between two matters, indicating that the first of them is the necessitating thing (*malzum*), and the second is its necessary consequence (*lazim*). The positing of this particle, its nature, and its uses in this connection are four.

It may connect two negations or two affirmations, or a necessitating affirmed thing with a necessary negated thing, or the reverse. By affirmation and negation here we mean the formal, verbal sense, not the meaning. The first kind is exemplified by: ﴿Say: If you possessed the treasuries of the mercy of my Lord, you would then withhold them for fear of spending.﴾ (17:100) And: ﴿If they had, when they wronged themselves, come to you and asked Allah's forgiveness, and the Messenger had asked forgiveness for them, they would have found Allah Accepting of repentance and Merciful.﴾ (4:64) And: ﴿If they had done what they were advised, it would have been better for them and stronger in firmness.﴾ (4:66) And similar verses.

The second kind: "If my stepdaughter were not in my guardianship, she would not be lawful to me," and "If Allah did not fear, He would not disobey Him."

The third kind: ﴿And if whatever trees on earth were pens and the sea [were ink], replenished thereafter by seven seas, the words of Allah would not be exhausted.﴾ (31:27)

The fourth kind: "If you did not sin, Allah would take you away and bring a people who sin, then seek forgiveness, and He would forgive them." This is the form in which they came in negation and affirmation.

As for its judgment, there are two matters. The first is the negation of the first, from the negation of the second, because the first is the necessitating thing and the second is its consequence, and the necessitating thing is absent when its consequence is absent. The second is the realization of the second from the realization of the first, because the realization of the necessitating thing entails the realization of its consequence. When you understand this, know that there is nothing in the nature or positing of *lau* that indicates the negation or affirmation of either of the two clauses. Its nature and reality is only to indicate the stated connection. But it is brought only for a connection that includes the negation or the realization of the consequent or the antecedent. From here the confusion arose. It is not brought merely for connection, regardless of whether the two clauses are affirmed or negated. When it enters upon two connected clauses in which the consequent is negated, the negation of the antecedent is derived from the logic of the connection, not from the particle itself.

The explanation: the verse ﴿If there had been in them [the heavens and the earth] gods besides Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ (21:22) does not derive the negation of the ruin from the particle *lau*. Rather, the particle enters upon two matters, one of which is known to be absent by sense perception, so it links it with what the speaker wants to negate, namely the plurality of gods. The logic of the connection requires the absence of the necessitating thing when its consequence is absent. If the consequence is definitely and sensibly absent, the necessitating thing is absent too, due to the absence of the consequence, not because of the particle. Here there are two matters: the connection understood from the particle, and the absence of the consequence known by the senses. In this way the absence of both the consequence and the necessitating thing should be understood from *lau*. From here they said: if it enters upon two affirmations, they become negated, meaning the second of them is known to be absent from outside, so the first is absent because of its absence. And if it enters upon two negations, it affirms them for the same reason, because it enters upon a necessitating thing that is realized externally, so its necessitating thing is realized. As in "If you did not sin." The necessitating thing here, namely the occurrence of sin, is realized among humans externally, so its necessary consequence is realized, namely the continuation of the human race and the non-removal of humanity. Because the connection was established between the absence of sin and the absence of the continuation, but the absence of sin is definitely absent, so its consequence, the absence of our removal, is absent. Thus sin is affirmed and continuation is affirmed. The negation of all four cases is understood in this way.

When this is understood: one necessary consequence may entail several necessitating things, as animality is necessary for the human and the horse and others. The speaker intends to affirm the connection between some of these necessitating things and the consequence, on the supposition of the absence of other ones. So his intention is that the connection exists on the supposition of the absence of that other necessitating thing. Thus no one imagines the absence of the consequence when a particular necessitating thing is negated, for the connection still exists without it.

On this basis, "If Allah did not fear, He would not disobey Him" and "If my stepdaughter were not in my guardianship, she would not be lawful to me" are to be understood.

For the absence of disobedience has several necessitating things: fear, love, and reverence. So if some of them, such as fear, were absent, the consequence would not be void, because it has other necessitating things besides it.

Likewise, if the girl's being a stepdaughter were absent, the prohibition would not be absent, because the connection exists between it and another attribute, namely fosterage, and that attribute is established. This category arises only for a consequence with several necessitating things, when the speaker intends to establish the connection on the supposition of the negation of some of them.

As for the verse ﴿And if whatever trees on earth were pens and the sea [were ink]...﴾ (31:27): the verse was brought to show that if the trees of the earth were pens and the seas were ink, and the words of Allah were written with them, the seas and pens would be exhausted, but the words of Allah would not be exhausted. So the verse was brought to show the connection between the non-exhaustion of His words and the condition that the trees are pens and the seas are ink for writing. If the connection is established on this supposition, which is the strongest possible supposition for exhaustion of what is written, then its establishment on other suppositions is more fitting.

We clarify this with an example that leads to understanding the intent of the verse. If you say to a man who gives nothing to anyone: "Even if you owned the entire world, you would not give anyone any of it," you intend that his non-giving is established even on the greatest supposition that would require giving. So you link his non-giving with the causes of giving, namely the abundance of what he owns. This shows that his non-giving is established on what is less than this supposition, and that non-giving is necessary under every supposition. Understand the parallel of this meaning in the verse: the non-exhaustion of Allah's words on the supposition that the trees are pens and the seas are ink to write with. If they are not exhausted on this supposition, their non-exhaustion is necessary for it, so how much more so for less than it. Understand this subtle point, which is not offered at every time and which you will hardly find in books. It is from Allah's opening and favor, so to Him belongs praise and grace, and we ask Him for more of His bounty.

Observe how the rational rule agreed with the grammatical rule, and the texts came in accordance with both together, without departing from the requirement of reason or language, and without distorting any text. Even if this commentary contained no other benefit than this one, it would be worth a journey. How much more so, when it contains precious insights that are only available to one who has attained them. As for one who is not among them, he thinks a pearl is glass, and a round perforated glass is a pearl, and he belittles the jeweler and claims he cannot tell the difference. And Allah is the Helper.

(Section)

Then reflect on the wisdom in the measures of night and day, and you will find them in utmost benefit and wisdom. If the length of the day and night were to increase or decrease beyond what has been decreed for them, the benefit would be lost and the wisdom would differ accordingly. Rather, He made their measure twenty-four hours, and the two exchange increase and decrease between them: whatever is added to one of them is taken from the other, and the other then returns and reclaims it from it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾.

On this there are two opinions:

The first is that the meaning is: the darkness of this one enters the place of the light of that one, and the light of this one enters the place of the darkness of the other, so that each of them enters the place of its counterpart.

On this view, the verse is general, applying to every night and day.

The second opinion is that one of them adds to itself what it lacks from the other, so that what is lost from one enters the other and does not vanish entirely.

On this view, the verse refers specifically to some hours of each of the night and the day at times other than the equinox, so it is specific in time and in the amount that enters one of them from the other. In the temperate regions, the greatest extent of the increase reaches fifteen hours, so the other becomes nine hours. If it exceeds that, that region deviates in heat or cold until it reaches a limit where a human cannot live and plants cannot grow. Every place that the sun never reaches has no animal or plant living in it, due to its extreme cold and dryness; and every place that the sun never leaves in this way is due to its extreme heat and dryness. The places in which animals and plants live are those over which the sun rises and sets, and the most balanced of them are the places in which the four seasons succeed one another, with two balanced seasons, autumn and spring.

(Chapter: That patience is half of faith, and faith is two halves: half patience and half gratitude.)

Several of the early scholars (al-salaf) said: "Patience is half of faith." Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Faith is two halves: half patience and half gratitude." For this reason Allah, glorified is He, combined patience and gratitude in His saying ﴿Indeed in that are signs for every patient one, grateful.﴾ in Surah Ibrahim, in Surah Ha Mim 'Ayn Sin Qaf, in Surah Saba', and in Surah Luqman. Several considerations have been mentioned for this division into halves.

The first: Faith is a name for the combination of speech, action and intention, and these return to two sides: doing and refraining. Doing is acting in obedience to Allah, and this is the reality of gratitude; refraining is patience in abstaining from disobedience. The whole of religion lies in these two things: doing what is commanded and avoiding what is forbidden.

(The second consideration)

Faith is built upon two pillars: certainty (yaqin) and patience (sabr), which are the two pillars mentioned in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We made from them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient, and they were certain of Our signs.﴾

By certainty one knows the reality of the command and prohibition, and of reward and punishment; and by patience one carries out what he is commanded and restrains himself from what he is forbidden. He cannot attain belief that the command and prohibition are from Allah, and that reward and punishment are real, except through certainty, and he cannot persist in doing what is commanded and restraining himself from what is forbidden except through patience. Thus patience became half of faith, and the second half is gratitude, by doing what is commanded and leaving what is prohibited.

(The third consideration)

Faith is speech and action; speech is the speech of the heart and the tongue, and action is the action of the heart and the limbs. The explanation: whoever knows Allah with his heart but does not affirm it with his tongue is not a believer, as He said about the people of Pharaoh ﴿And they denied them while their souls were convinced of them.﴾

And as He said about 'Ad and Thamud ﴿And 'Ad and Thamud—and it has become clear to you from their dwellings. And Satan made their deeds attractive to them and averted them from the way, though they were discerning.﴾

And Musa said to Pharaoh ﴿You certainly know that these have not sent down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as evidence.﴾ These people possessed the speech of the heart, which is knowledge and cognizance, yet they were not believers by that. Likewise, whoever says with his tongue what is not in his heart is not a believer by that, but is among the hypocrites. Likewise, whoever knows with his heart and affirms with his tongue is not, by that mere act, a believer until he brings the action of the heart: love, hatred, loyalty and enmity. So he loves Allah and His Messenger, allies himself with the friends of Allah, opposes His enemies, submits his heart to Allah alone, and submits to following His Messenger, obeying him and adhering to his law, outwardly and inwardly. And when he does this, his perfection of faith is not complete until he does what is commanded.

These four pillars are the pillars of faith upon which its structure rests, and they return to knowledge and action. Action includes restraining the self, which is the object of prohibition. Both of these are attained only through patience. Thus faith became two halves: the first is patience, and the second arises from it, namely knowledge and action.

(The fourth consideration)

The soul has two powers: the power of advancing (iqdam) and the power of withdrawing (ihjam). It constantly oscillates between the rulings of these two powers, advancing toward what it loves and withdrawing from what it dislikes. The whole of religion is advancing and withdrawing: advancing to obedience and withdrawing from the disobediences of Allah, and neither of these can be achieved except through patience.

The fifth consideration: The whole of religion is desire (raghba) and fear (rahba). The believer is one who desires and fears. Allah, the Exalted, said ﴿Indeed they used to hasten to good works and call upon Us in desire and fear.﴾ And in the supplication at sleep narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih:

"O Allah, I have submitted myself to You, turned my face to You, entrusted my affair to You, and leaned my back upon You, in desire of You and fear of You."

You will never find the believer except desiring and fearing. Desire and fear cannot stand except on the leg of patience: his fear compels him to patience, and his desire leads him to gratitude.

(The sixth consideration)

Everything the servant undertakes in this abode does not fall outside of what benefits him in this world and the Hereafter, or harms him in this world and the Hereafter, or benefits him in one of the two abodes and harms him in the other. The noblest of these divisions is that he does what benefits him in the Hereafter and abandons what harms him there, and this is the reality of faith. Doing what benefits him is gratitude, and abandoning what harms him is patience.

(The seventh consideration)

The servant is never free of a command he performs, a prohibition he avoids, and a decree that befalls him. Its obligations among these three are patience and gratitude.

Doing what is commanded is gratitude, avoiding what is forbidden is [also gratitude/restraint], and patience upon what is decreed is patience.

(The eighth consideration)

The servant has two callers: a caller who calls him to this world and its desires, pleasures and delights, and a caller who calls him to Allah and the Hereafter and what He has prepared therein for His friends of lasting bliss. Disobeying the caller of desire and passion is patience, and answering the caller of Allah and the Hereafter is gratitude.

(The ninth consideration)

Religion revolves around two principles: resolve ('azm) and steadfastness (thabat), which are the two principles mentioned in the hadith narrated by Ahmad and al-Nasa'i from the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Allah, I ask You for steadfastness in the matter and resolve upon right guidance." The root of gratitude is the soundness of resolve, and the root of patience is the strength of steadfastness. Whenever the servant is strengthened with resolve and steadfastness, he has been strengthened with help and success.

The tenth consideration: Religion is built upon two principles: truth (haqq) and patience, which are the two mentioned in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And they counselled one another to truth, and counselled one another to patience.﴾

Since what is required of the servant is to act upon the truth in himself and to implement it among people, and this is the reality of gratitude, he cannot do that except by being patient in it. Thus patience is half of faith. And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best.

[Section: Self-Deception Regarding the Causes]

The second matter is that one must beware of deceiving oneself about these causes, and this is among the most important matters. A servant knows that disobedience and heedlessness are among the causes that harm him in this world and the Hereafter, and that this is inevitable. Yet his own soul deceives him: sometimes by relying on God's pardon and forgiveness, sometimes by postponing repentance and seeking forgiveness only with the tongue, sometimes by performing recommended acts, sometimes by knowledge, sometimes by arguing from divine decree (qadar), sometimes by arguing from those like and similar to himself, and at other times by imitating the great.

Many people think that if they do what they do and then say, "I seek God's forgiveness," the effect of the sin disappears and this cancels that. A man among those who claim to be jurists told me: "I do what I do, then I say 'Glory be to God and praise be to Him' one hundred times, and all of that is forgiven," as it is authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever says 'Glory be to God and praise be to Him' one hundred times in a day, his sins are removed, even if they were like the foam of the sea." Another man from the people of Makkah told me: "When one of us does what he does, he bathes, circumambulates the House seven times, and that is erased from him." Another told me: "It is authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said:

'A servant committed a sin and said, "O Lord, I have committed a sin, so forgive me." God forgave his sin. Then he remained for as long as God willed, then committed another sin and said, "O Lord, I have committed a sin, so forgive me." God, Mighty and Majestic, said: "My servant knows that he has a Lord who forgives sins and takes account for them. I have forgiven My servant, so let him do as he wills."'"

He said: "I have no doubt that I have a Lord who forgives sins and takes account for them." This kind of people has attached itself to texts about hope, relied upon them, and clung to them with both hands. When he is reproached for his sins and for persisting in them, he recites to you what he has memorized of the vastness of God's mercy and forgiveness and the texts of hope. Among the ignorant of this kind of people there are strange and wondrous sayings in this regard, such as the saying of one of them:

*"Multiply your sins as much as you can,*
*When you are to meet a Generous One."*

And the saying of another: "Abstaining from sins is ignorance of the vastness of God's pardon."

And another said: "Leaving sins is audacity toward God's forgiveness and a belittling of it."

Muhammad ibn Hazm said: "I saw one of these people say in his supplication: 'O God, I seek refuge in You from being protected (from sin).'"

**Clinging to Compulsion (jabr)**

Among these deluded people are those who cling to the doctrine of compulsion (jabr), holding that the servant has no action or choice whatsoever, and that he is compelled to commit acts of disobedience.

**Clinging to Postponement (irja')**

Among these are those who are deceived by the doctrine of postponement (irja'), which holds that faith is merely assent, that deeds are not part of faith, and that the faith of the most wicked of people is like the faith of Gabriel and Michael.

Among these are those who are deceived by loving the poor, the shaykhs and the righteous, by frequently visiting their graves, by humbling themselves before them, by seeking their intercession (shafa'ah), by seeking nearness to God through them (tawassul), and by asking God by their right over Him and their sanctity with Him.

Among them are those who are deceived by their fathers and forefathers, believing that these have a rank and righteousness with God, so that they will not leave him to be saved, as one witnesses in the courts of kings. For kings grant their close associates the sins of their sons and relatives, and if one of them falls into a grievous matter, his father and grandfather rescue him by their influence and standing.

**Being Deceived About God**

Among them are those who are deceived by the belief that God, Mighty and Majestic, is free of needing to punish him, that His punishment does not increase His kingdom in anything, and that His mercy toward him does not diminish His kingdom in anything. So he says: "I am in need of His mercy, and He is the most self-sufficient of the self-sufficient." But if a poor, needy man, in need of a drink of water, were in the house of one who had a flowing stream, that man would not withhold it from him. God is more generous and more vast. Forgiveness does not diminish Him in anything, and punishment does not increase His kingdom in anything.

**Being Deceived by Corrupt Understanding of the Qur'an and Sunnah**

Among them are those who are deceived by a corrupt understanding that they and their like have derived from the texts of the Qur'an and Sunnah, and they rely on it, as some rely on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be satisfied﴾ [al-Duha 93:5].

He said: "He will not be satisfied while there is anyone of his community in the Fire." This is among the most shameful ignorance and the clearest lie against him, for he is satisfied with what his Lord is satisfied with. God, Exalted, is satisfied by the punishment of the oppressors, the wicked, the treacherous, and those who persist in major sins. So far be it from His Messenger to be satisfied with what his Lord is not satisfied with, may He be blessed and exalted.

And like some people's reliance on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, God forgives all sins﴾ [al-Zumar 39:53].

This too is among the most shameful ignorance, for shirk is included in this verse, since it is the head and foundation of sins. There is no disagreement that this verse concerns those who repent, for He forgives the sin of every penitent, whatever sin it was. If the verse were concerning those who do not repent, all the texts of warning (wa'id) would be nullified.

And the hadiths about bringing out a group of monotheists from the Fire by intercession.

This person has only been brought to this error by the lack of his knowledge and understanding, for here He, glorified, generalized and left it unrestricted, so it is known that He meant the penitent. In Surat al-Nisa', He specified and restricted, saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that He be associated with, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:48]. Thus God, glorified, informed that He does not forgive shirk, and informed that He forgives what is below it. Had this been concerning the penitent, He would not have distinguished between shirk and other sins.

Like the deception of some ignorant people by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿O human, what has deceived you concerning your Generous Lord?﴾ [al-Infitar 82:6], so he says: "His generosity." Some of them even say: "He taught the deceived one his argument." This is an ugly ignorance. Rather, the deception (al-ghurur) that deceived him concerning his Lord is the Shaytan, his own commanding soul (nafs ammarah bi al-su'), his ignorance, and his desire. And the Exalted used the word "Generous," which refers to the Great Lord who is obeyed, and one should not be deceived by Him or neglect His right. This deceived person has placed deception in other than its proper place, and has been deceived by one whom he should not be deceived by.

Like the deception of some by the saying of the Exalted about the Fire: ﴿None will burn therein except the most wretched, who denied and turned away﴾ [al-Layl 92:15-16], and His saying: ﴿It is prepared for the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:24].

This deceived person did not realize that His saying ﴿So I have warned you of a Fire blazing﴾ refers to a specific Fire among the levels of Hell. And even if it were the whole of Hell, He, glorified, did not say "none will enter it," but said ﴿none will burn therein except the most wretched﴾. And from the absence of burning, it does not follow the absence of entering, for burning (al-sally) is more specific than entering, and negating the more specific does not necessitate negating the more general.

Moreover, if this deceived person had reflected on the verse that follows it, he would have known that he is not included in it, and it is not guaranteed for him that he will be spared it.

As for His saying about the Fire, ﴿It is prepared for the disbelievers﴾, He has said of Paradise: ﴿It is prepared for the righteous﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:133]. The preparation of the Fire for the disbelievers does not preclude that wrongdoers and sinners enter it, and the preparation of Paradise for the righteous does not preclude that one enter it who has in his heart the least weight of a mustard seed of faith and never did any good.

And like the deception of some by fasting the Day of 'Ashura' or the Day of 'Arafah, to the extent that some say: "The Day of 'Ashura' expiates all the sins of the year, and the fasting of 'Arafah remains as an addition to the reward." This deceived person did not realize that fasting Ramadan and the five daily prayers are greater and more exalted than fasting the Day of 'Arafah and the Day of 'Ashura', and they only expiate what is between them when major sins are avoided.

Ramadan to Ramadan and Friday to Friday do not have the strength to expiate minor sins unless abstention from major sins is joined to them. Thus the combination of the two matters becomes strong enough to expiate minor sins.

So how can the fasting of a voluntary day expiate every major sin the servant committed while he persists in it and does not repent of it? This is impossible. Yet it is not impossible that the fasting of the Day of 'Arafah and the Day of 'Ashura expiates all the sins of the year in their generality, and that it is among the texts of promise that have conditions and impediments, and that persistence in major sins is an impediment to expiation. So if he does not persist in major sins, the fasting and the absence of persistence combine and cooperate for the general expiation, just as Ramadan and the five prayers, along with avoiding major sins, cooperate and assist one another in expiating minor sins. Moreover, God, glorified, has said: ﴿If you avoid the major sins you are forbidden, We will expiate from you your misdeeds﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:31].

Thus it is known that making one thing a cause of expiation does not prevent it from cooperating with another cause for expiation, and that expiation with the combination of two causes is stronger and more complete than with either one alone. The more the causes of expiation are strengthened, the stronger, more complete and more comprehensive it becomes.

**Good Opinion of God (husn al-zann)**

And like some people's reliance on his saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, relating from his Lord: "I am according to My servant's opinion of Me, so let him think of Me as he wills," meaning: whatever he thinks of Me, I shall do to him accordingly. There is no doubt that good opinion of God comes only with good deeds, for the doer of good has a good opinion of his Lord: that He will reward him for his good, not break His promise, and accept his repentance.

As for the evildoer who persists in major sins, injustice and transgressions, the desolation (wahsha) of sins, injustice and the unlawful prevents him from having a good opinion of his Lord. This is evident in the visible world: a runaway slave who has left his master's obedience does not have a good opinion of him, and good opinion never combines with the desolation of wrongdoing, for the evildoer feels desolate in proportion to his evil. The people with the best opinion of their Lord are the most obedient to Him.

As al-Hasan al-Basri said: "The believer has a good opinion of his Lord, so he does good deeds; and the wicked person has a bad opinion of his Lord, so he does evil deeds."

How can one who is distant from Him, dwelling and roaming in what displeases Him and angers Him, exposed to His curse, whose right and command have become insignificant to him so that he neglects them, whose prohibition has become insignificant to him so that he commits it and persists in it, have a good opinion of his Lord?

How can one who wages war against Him, opposes His friends, allies with His enemies, denies the attributes of His perfection, has a bad opinion of what He described Himself with and what His Messenger (ﷺ) described Him with, and in his ignorance thinks that the apparent meaning of that is misguidance and disbelief, have a good opinion of his Lord? And how can one have a good opinion of his Lord who thinks that He does not speak, does not command, does not forbid, is not pleased, and does not become angry?

God has said concerning one who doubted that His hearing reaches even some particulars, the secret of speech: ﴿And that was your opinion which you thought of your Lord; it has ruined you, and you have become among the losers﴾ [Fussilat 41:23].

Since they thought that God, glorified, does not know much of what they do, this was an evil opinion of their Lord, and that opinion ruined them. This is the case of everyone who denies the attributes of His perfection and the descriptions of His majesty, and describes Him with what is not fitting for Him. If such a person thinks that He will admit him into Paradise, this is delusion and self-deception from his own soul, and a whispering from the Shaytan, not good opinion of his Lord.

So reflect on this point, and reflect on how greatly one needs it. How can there combine in a servant's heart the certainty that he will meet God, that God hears and sees his place, knows his secret and his public, that nothing of his affair is hidden from Him, that he will be made to stand before Him and be questioned about all he did, while he remains persisting in what displeases Him, neglecting His commands, and disregarding His rights, and yet he has a good opinion of Him? Is this anything other than one of the deceptions of the souls and the delusion of wishful thinking?

Abu Umamah ibn Sahl ibn Hunayf said: "Uthman? No. Abu Umamah ibn Sahl ibn Hunayf said: 'I and Urwah ibn al-Zubayr entered upon A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, and she said: "If you had seen the Messenger of Allah ﷺ during an illness of his, and I had six or seven dinars, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded me to distribute them. She said: The pain of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ occupied me until Allah granted him recovery. Then he asked me about them and said: What did you do? Did you distribute the six dinars? I said: No, by Allah, your pain occupied me. She said: So he called for them, placed them in his palm, and said: What would the opinion of the Prophet of Allah be if he met Allah while these were with him?" And in another wording: "What would the opinion of Muhammad be of his Lord if he met Allah while these were with him?"'"

So, by Allah, what is the opinion of the people of major sins and the wrongdoers of Allah when they meet Him while the injustices against people are with them? If their saying, "We have held good opinion of You, for You will not punish a wrongdoer or a sinner," would benefit them, then the servant may do whatever he wishes and commit everything Allah has forbidden him, and let him think well of Allah, for the Fire will not touch him. Glory be to Allah! How far delusion (ghurur, self-deception) can carry a servant! Indeed Ibrahim said to his people: ﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than Allah, that you desire? So what is your opinion of the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [al-Saffat: 86-87].

That is, what is your opinion of what He will do to you when you meet Him, having worshipped other than Him?

Whoever reflects on this matter with true reflection will know that good opinion of Allah is itself good action. The servant is moved to good action by his opinion of his Lord, that He will reward him for his deeds, recompense him for them, and accept them from him. So what moved him to act is good opinion; whenever his good opinion is good, his action is good. Otherwise, good opinion accompanied by following one's desires is incapacity (ajz), as in the hadith of al-Tirmidhi and the Musnad from the hadith of Shaddad ibn Aws, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The wise (al-kayyis) is one who holds himself accountable and works for what comes after death, and the incapable is one who follows his desires and wishes against Allah."

In sum, good opinion occurs only when the means of salvation are established. But when the means of destruction are established, good opinion cannot be realized.

The difference between good opinion and delusion

If it is said: Rather, it is possible, and the basis of good opinion is the vastness of Allah's forgiveness, His mercy, His pardon, and His generosity, and that His mercy precedes His wrath, and that punishment does not benefit Him, and pardon does not harm Him.

It is said: The matter is as you say, and Allah is above that and more exalted, more noble, more generous, and more merciful. But one places that in its proper place that is fitting for it. He, glory be to Him, is described with wisdom, might, retribution, severity of seizing, and punishing whoever deserves punishment. So if the basis of good opinion were merely His attributes and names, then the righteous and the wicked, the believer and the disbeliever, His ally and His enemy would all share in it. The names and attributes of Allah do not benefit the criminal, who has returned with His wrath and anger, exposed himself to His curse, fallen into what He has forbidden, and violated His sanctities. Rather, good opinion benefits only the one who repents, regrets, and gives up sin, replaces an evil deed with a good one, faces the rest of his life with goodness and obedience, and then holds good opinion. This is good opinion, while the former is delusion. And Allah is the One sought for help.

Do not drag out this section, for the need for it is great for everyone who distinguishes between good opinion of Allah and delusion about Him. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who emigrated and struggled in the way of Allah, those hope for the mercy of Allah, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 218]. So He made these the people of hope, not the idle and the defiant.

He the Exalted said: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they were tried, then struggled and were patient, indeed your Lord, after that, is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 110].

So He, glory be to Him, informed that after these things He is Forgiving and Merciful to those who do them. The scholar places hope in its proper places, while the ignorant deluded person places it in other than its proper places.
